claims.text: The material family is FCC high-entropy alloys derived from the Fe-Co-Ni system, specifically equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The primary property targeted for improvement is magnetic response.
The specifically targeted magnetic properties are saturation magnetization and the orbital magnetic-moment contribution.
The orbital magnetic moment is critical for high-temperature magnetic applications.
The orbital contribution is quenched or difficult to isolate in the paramagnetic state because of longitudinal spin fluctuations and the electronic interplay among 3d elements.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations induce sizable magnetic moments on Co, Cr, and Ni in both FCC and HCP CoCrFeMnNi.
The orbital contribution to the total magnetic moment has not been fully quantified or controlled as a function of temperature.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi generally forms a chemically disordered FCC solid solution at ambient pressure over a wide temperature range below its solidus.
First-principles alloy theory can be used to model paramagnetic CoCrFeMnNi while explicitly accounting for temperature-dependent longitudinal spin fluctuations.
The HCP phase is energetically preferred over the FCC phase at cryogenic temperatures.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations and FCC-HCP phase competition modulate local magnetic environments and induced moment magnitudes.
Strong spin-orbit coupling and dynamic longitudinal spin fluctuations suppress or destabilize the orbital moment.
The orbital moment is coupled to longitudinal spin fluctuations and to the local FCC-versus-HCP crystal-field symmetry.
Crystal fields commonly quench orbital moments in 3d transition-metal alloys.
Chemical disorder and longitudinal spin fluctuations can reduce orbital quenching and produce a nonzero, temperature-dependent orbital moment.
The orbital moment will be significant, smaller than the spin moment, and increase with temperature as longitudinal spin fluctuations become activated.
The total magnetic moment will vary non-monotonically with temperature because of FCC-HCP phase stability changes.
At cryogenic temperatures, HCP symmetry may enhance the orbital contribution while reducing the overall magnetization.
Experimental finite-temperature magnetic data for single-phase CoCrFeMnNi are incomplete.
Existing models often assume quenched orbital moments or neglect longitudinal spin fluctuations in the paramagnetic state.

contradictions.description: The orbital contribution is predicted to increase with temperature, while also being described as enhanced in the cryogenic HCP phase; the relative reference states needed to reconcile these trends are not specified.
